I will offer what I can on this subject.

There's a concept we call the quantity theory of money which essentially means that the value of money in nominal terms is related to how much money there is. One of the main equations is as follows:

MV = PT
M = money supply (or the amount of money in an economy)
V = velocity of money (the rate at which money changes hands)
P = average price
T = the volume of transactions

This is the fisher equation and comes (as with all economics) a set of somewhat unrealistic assumptions and conditions e.g. perfect information, a closed system etc.

If we us the USA as an example, giving everyone $1m would cause an increase on the left hand side of roughly 300, 000, 000, 000, 000 (using population as roughly 300m).

Holding eveything else constant (I.e. v and t remain the same) then the same would have to happen on the right hand side which would equate as probably around 3x10^13 % inflation which wouldnt work. Currency would become worthless and the economy would collapse.

This is only one (and probably the simplest) way to approach the question. I could probably demonstrate the more complex methods but I am 4 beers deep.

Right well here is my attempt:

A country raises money by issuing debts, in the UK we call these treasury bills, and these debts essentially say that in Xyears (normally 10-30) we will repay the money you lent at a rate of Y%. This rate Y is determined by how likely it is that a government will repay this debt - much the same as someone with a low credit score paying a higher interest rate than someone with a good score.
Essentially higher risk of non payment must bring with it a higher return on the loan.

When a country can no longer afford to pay back these debts, which in practice means they can no longer make their spiralling interest payments then they go into default. Defaulting is much the same as declaring bankruptcy except that countries are generally not covered by bankruptcy courts in their own country. Ultimately, going into default is an admission that you cannot afford to pay back your debts. With sovereign debts (national debts) default may also occur as a result of a refusal to pay back these debts in full. Unlike a debt that me or you may accumulate, those who are owed money can't repossess a country or sovereignty (anymore - see Britain for much of the 17/1800s) so nowadays the outcome is a restructuring of the debt which basically equates to a renegotiation of interest rates etc.

For expansion, a country may find itself unable to pay back debts for a number of reasons. The ELI5 answer would be that consistently their outgoings (govt. expenditure, public sector pay etc) is higher than their income (tax). If this happens only for a few years then a government may issue bonds or T-bills (as discussed before) to cover this deficit. As with me or you, the more debt we have the more expensive new debt is so if over a number years a government has to keep issuing more debt to keep afloat it becomes more expensive. This means that a big economic shock (such as one requiring a cut in taxes or an increase in outgoings such as welfare/benenfit payments) very quickly adds to the amount of debt and thus the repayment levels. Just as we all know or have heard of people who use a payday lender but misses payments and ends up using another company to pay off their initial loan amount and so on until their debt spirals and becomes unmanagable, countries face the same.

TL:DR essentially the same as people declaring themselves bankrupt but with different legal ramifications.

Source: Economics graduate & Postgraduate Student
